summary:
Fire behaves very differently in microgravity. Without buoyancy, flames become spherical, oxygen reaches them mainly by diffusion, and Earth-based intuition no longer applies. Inside a sealed spacecraft, understanding this is a safety requirement.

Flame in Freefall is an open, reproducible workflow for exploring NASA’s public combustion data from the Physical Sciences Informatics repository, starting with the FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments. It takes raw experiment files and produces cleaned, documented data. It then extracts flame-size histories, fits the d²-law burning rate, compares conditions such as fuel and oxygen level, and flags unusual runs for expert review. Results appear in an interactive dashboard, with every output traced back to a source file and stated with its limitations.

The project makes valuable open data easier for students and researchers to use, supporting fire-safety research for future crewed missions. It is an offline research aid, not a fire detector.
details:
Fire behaves very differently in microgravity, and in a sealed spacecraft, understanding it is a safety requirement. NASA has studied this on the International Space Station and made much of the experiment data public, but turning that data into trends and insights still takes specialist knowledge. Flame in Freefall, built by Team Rapax, is an open, reproducible workflow that takes public NASA combustion data and produces interpretable trends and caveated research fire-safety indicators. It is a research aid for offline analysis, not a real-time fire detector.

What it does and how it works

Flame in Freefall is an open, reproducible workflow that turns NASA’s public microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insight. It starts with the FLEX-2 droplet experiments in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and works in six steps. It collects the open data, organises and documents each file, analyses flame size and burning rate, detects trends and unusual runs, explains them with combustion physics, and reports research safety indicators with their caveats. The core physics is the droplet d²-law (D² = D₀² − K t), which gives a burning-rate constant K for each fuel and oxygen level. An interactive web page lets anyone see how the model behaves by changing droplet size and K.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes complex experiment data easier for students and researchers to explore. Every output traces back to a source file and states its limitations. It also speeds up first-pass analysis by flagging unusual runs for expert review, and because it is open, anyone can repeat the analysis. We want it to support fire-safety research for future crewed missions by making NASA’s open combustion data easier to use and interpret. It is a research aid for offline analysis, not a real-time fire detector, and any operational use would come only after independent validation.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The project website is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with an inline SVG chart, and is hosted on Netlify. The data comes from NASA PSI and its public AWS Open Data bucket. For analysis, our team used [list your real tools, such as Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn and Plotly], on [your laptops or computers]. We also used Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, to help build the presentation and website.

Creativity

Instead of building another flame simulator, we focused on accessibility. The project takes a newcomer from raw public files to interpretable trends, with every limitation stated. It is also honest by design: the demo is clearly labelled as a physics-model simulation and not NASA data, and the novelty we claim is in integration and accessibility, not in new physics.

Factors we considered

We considered the physics, because microgravity changes how oxygen reaches a flame (by diffusion instead of buoyancy), so Earth-based intuition does not carry over. The model also assumes quasi-steady burning, spherical symmetry and constant properties. On data quality, we planned for missing frames, invalid values and consistent units. For valid testing, we split data by experiment run, not by frame, so correlated frames don’t leak between training and test sets. We also accepted the limits of the work: few runs and conditions, measurement uncertainty, and no generalisation beyond the tested conditions. Above all, this is not an operational alarm, and we claim nothing beyond what the data supports.
